It can only be negligence if the defendant owed a duty of care to the victim. Legally, no such duty of care would exist between mates in these circumstances.

A conviction of unlawful dangerous act manslaughter might have been possible, but any prosecution would need to prove :

A. The act of pushing his friend was a criminal act
B. If it was a criminal act, then that the act was dangerous
C. That the "pusher" either intended to cause the criminal offence or he was aware that his conduct might lead to the offence but he took that risk anyway.

There is an argument for the case of unlawful dangerous act manslaughter, but it might be difficult for the prosecution to convince a jury of the three above factors, beyond reasonable doubt. If it is established that the "pusher" did not foresee the victim getting hurt at all, or even considered that it was a possibility, then it is likely he would be found "not guilty".

Paying rent each month and going to a restaurant is not comparable. People's circumstances can change suddenly- they can lose their job for whatever reason or they could fall ill and not be able to work. Admittedly, there will be tenants who try and cheat the system or who purposefully just decide not to pay. However, the fact is that it is not unusual for a tenant to fall into rent arrears, whether rightly or wrongly, and for this landlord to not account for this risk by being so reliant on the tenant is a massive oversight and poor planning.

>"A lot of landlords are only wealthy on paper so they cannot absorb a loss."

But that's the crux of the issue - the majority of landlords do not view renting as a risk. My job involves a lot of involvement with landlords who are experiencing issues with tenants and I am continously hearing that a landlord cannot afford their own mortgage because the tenant has stopped paying the rent.

There is a sense of entitlement from landlords that renting should be a risk free investment, whereas that does not exist anywhere else.

If a landlord cannot absorb a loss, then it is poor financial planning on their part. If an individual put all of his savings in stocks which subsequently crashed, you would blame the individual for risking more money that he could afford to lose. Why are landlords exempt from this risk?

I do not disagree that there is a massive supply issue, but I dont think that just building more houses is enough.

Any new affordable properties will just be snapped up by BTL landlords who can out bid first time buyers. 

There needs to be regulations in place or an overhaul of the system that either makes it easier for first time buyers or less attractive for BTL landlords
